claim: TERT was transcriptionally altered depending on telomere length (TL).
source: We found TERT was transcriptionally altered depending on telomere length (TL).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by multiple experimental results throughout the manuscript.

claim: TL-dependent binding of TRF2 occurs between telomeres and the TERT promoter.
source: This resulted from TL-dependent binding of TRF2 between telomeres and the TERT promoter.
evidence: Stated in abstract and demonstrated through ChIP experiments in multiple cell lines.

claim: TERT promoter-bound TRF2 was non-telomeric and did not involve the looping of telomeres to the TERT promoter.
source: TERT promoter-bound TRF2 was non-telomeric and did not involve the looping of telomeres to the TERT promoter.
evidence: Demonstrated through experiments with artificially inserted TERT promoter >40 Mb from telomeres and absence of other telomeric factors.

claim: Telomere elongation in HT1080, HCT116, and MDA-MB-231 cell lines resulted in an increase in TERT expression.
source: Cell lines from different tissue types fibrosarcoma (HT1080), colon cancer (HCT116), and breast cancer (MDA-MB-231), engineered for either telomere elongation/shortening, gave an increase/decrease in TERT, respectively.
evidence: Demonstrated through multiple experimental models including TERT overexpression, GTR oligonucleotides, and TERC knockdown.

claim: Telomere shortening in HT1080, HCT116, and MDA-MB-231 cell lines resulted in a decrease in TERT expression.
source: Cell lines from different tissue types fibrosarcoma (HT1080), colon cancer (HCT116), and breast cancer (MDA-MB-231), engineered for either telomere elongation/shortening, gave an increase/decrease in TERT, respectively.
evidence: Demonstrated through telomere trimming with Cas9 and TERC knockdown experiments.

claim: TERT promoter-bound non-telomeric TRF2 recruits the canonical PRC2-complex, inducing repressor histone H3K27-trimethylation in a TL-dependent fashion.
source: Mechanistically, we show TERT promoter-bound non-telomeric TRF2 recruits the canonical PRC2-complex, inducing repressor histone H3K27-trimethylation in a TL-dependent fashion.
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP experiments showing REST and EZH2 recruitment and H3K27me3 deposition correlating with TRF2 binding.

claim: An exogenously inserted TERT reporter showed TL-dependent promoter activity.
source: This was further supported by TL-dependent promoter activity from an exogenously inserted TERT reporter.
evidence: Demonstrated using TERT promoter-Gaussia luciferase reporter inserted at CCR5 locus, 46 Mb from nearest telomere.

claim: Increase in TL over days followed by a gradual decline resulted in activation followed by repression of TERT in a concerted manner.
source: Increase in TL over days followed by a gradual decline, resulted in activation followed by repression of TERT in a concerted manner, further implicating TL as a key factor for TERT regulation.
evidence: Demonstrated in doxycycline-inducible TERT models in HT1080 and MDA-MB-231 cells with temporal analysis.

claim: On reprogramming primary fibroblasts to induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), TRF2 loss from the TERT promoter was evident along with telomere elongation and TERT upregulation.
source: Notably, on reprogramming primary fibroblasts to induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), TRF2 loss from the TERT promoter was evident along with telomere elongation and TERT upregulation.
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP and expression analysis comparing foreskin fibroblasts to derived iPSCs.

claim: On telomere shortening in iPSCs, TERT promoter-bound TRF2 was restored with a marked reduction in TERT.
source: Conversely, on telomere shortening in iPSCs, TERT promoter-bound TRF2 was restored with a marked reduction in TERT, further supporting the causal role of TL in TERT transcription.
evidence: Demonstrated using telomere-specific sgRNA-guided CRISPR-Cas9 to trim telomeres in iPSCs.

claim: Telomeres are nucleoprotein structures comprising guanine-rich DNA sequences at the end of linear chromosomes.
source: Telomeres are nucleoprotein structures comprising guanine-rich DNA sequences at the end of linear chromosomes (Rhodes et al., 2002; O'Sullivan and Karlseder, 2010; Shay and Wright, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited references.

claim: TERT is necessary for replicating telomeric repeats to maintain telomeres.
source: The catalytic subunit of the ribonucleoprotein telomerase, human telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) is necessary for replicating telomeric repeats to maintain telomeres (Greider and Blackburn, 1985; Blackburn, 2001; Autexier and Lue, 2006; Smith et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited references.

claim: Most cancer cells maintain telomeres through reactivation of TERT in approximately 90% of cancers.
source: Most cancer cells, in contrast to normal adult somatic cells, maintain telomeres through reactivation of TERT (~90% of cancers); alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) is used in other cases (Shay and Bacchetti, 1997; Pandita et al., 2015; Heaphy et al., 2011; Akincilar et al., 2016b; Sharma and Chowdhury, 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited references.

claim: TERT is tightly regulated at the epigenetic, transcriptional, and translational levels.
source: TERT, therefore, is tightly regulated at the epigenetic, transcriptional, and translational levels (Roake and Artandi, 2020; Cong et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited references.

claim: Physical looping of telomeres (TPE-OLD) was shown to extend up to 10 Mb of telomeres (sub-telomeric).
source: Physical looping of telomeres, reported as the Telomeric Position Effect-over-long-distance (TPE-OLD) was shown to extend up to 10 Mb of telomeres (sub-telomeric).
evidence: This refers to previously published work on TPE-OLD mechanism.

claim: The TERT loci (~1.2 Mb away from telomeres) was shown to be repressed through TPE-OLD.
source: The TERT loci (~1.2 Mb away from telomeres) was shown to be repressed through (TPE-OLD) (Robin et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2016; Kim and Shay, 2018) loss of looping in short telomeres induced TERT.
evidence: This refers to previously published work on TPE-OLD mechanism.

claim: Non-telomeric binding of TRF2 was found to be extensive (>20,000 sites), spread across the genome, including promoters.
source: First, non-telomeric binding of TRF2 was found to be extensive (>20,000 sites), spread across the genome, including promoters, and affected the epigenetic regulation of genes (Mukherjee et al., 2018b; Mukherjee et al., 2019; Purohit et al., 2018).
evidence: This refers to previously published work by the authors.

claim: The shortening or elongation of telomeres led to the release or sequestration of telomeric TRF2, respectively, thereby increasing or decreasing the availability of TRF2 at non-telomeric promoters.
source: Second, the shortening or elongation of telomeres led to the release or sequestration of telomeric TRF2, respectively, thereby increasing or decreasing the availability of TRF2 at non-telomeric promoters and affecting gene expression (Mukherjee et al., 2018b; Mukherjee et al., 2021).
evidence: This refers to the TSP model previously published by the authors.

claim: HT1080-LT cells had significantly reduced occupancy of TRF2 on the TERT promoter compared to HT1080-ST cells.
source: Chromatin-immunoprecipitation (ChIP) of TRF2 gave significantly reduced occupancy of TRF2 on the TERT promoter in HT1080-LT compared to HT1080-ST cells (Figure 2B, ChIP-qPCR spanning 0–300 bp upstream of transcription start site, TSS).
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: H3K27me3 mark was significantly reduced in HT1080-LT relative to ST cells.
source: With TL elongation, the H3K27me3 mark was significantly reduced in HT1080-LT relative to the ST cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: TERT transcription was enhanced by >threefolds in HT1080-LT relative to ST cells.
source: As expected from reduced promoter H3K27 trimethylation, TERT transcription was enhanced by >threefolds in HT1080-LT relative to ST cells; 3'UTR-specific primers were used to distinguish from exogenously expressed TERT (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated through qRT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: MDA-MB-231-LT cells had lower TRF2 binding at the TERT promoter compared to MDA-MB-231-ST cells.
source: MDA-MB-231-LT cells had lower TRF2 binding at the TERT promoter compared to MDA-MB-231-ST cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: H3K27 trimethylation at the TERT promoter was reduced in MDA-MB-231-LT compared to MDA-MB-231-ST cells.
source: Accordingly, H3K27 trimethylation at the TERT promoter was reduced and TERT upregulated by ~threefolds in MDA-MB-231-LT compared to MDA-MB-231-ST cells (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: TERT was upregulated by approximately threefolds in MDA-MB-231-LT compared to MDA-MB-231-ST cells.
source: Accordingly, H3K27 trimethylation at the TERT promoter was reduced and TERT upregulated by ~threefolds in MDA-MB-231-LT compared to MDA-MB-231-ST cells (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: Demonstrated through qRT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: HCT116-ST cells had higher TRF2 binding on the TERT promoter compared to HCT116-LT cells in both telomere-shortened models.
source: The ST cells in both TL-shortened models had higher TRF2 binding on the TERT promoter compared to the HCT116-LT cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 2B for both CRISPR-Cas9 and TERC knockdown models.

claim: HCT116-ST cells showed higher repressor H3K27me3 mark at the TERT promoter compared to HCT116-LT cells.
source: Also, we found a higher repressor H3K27me3 mark at the TERT promoter, as expected from increased TRF2, in ST compared to its LT counterpart in both the HCT116 models (Figure 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: TERT expression was reduced by more than twofold in HCT116-ST relative to HCT116-LT cells.
source: As expected, an increase in the H3K27me3 repressor mark at the TERT promoter resulted in > twofold reduced TERT expression in ST relative to the HCT116-LT cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated through qRT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: REST showed enhanced occupancy at the TERT promoter in HT1080-ST relative to HT1080-LT cells.
source: ChIP of REST showed enhanced occupancy at the TERT promoter in ST relative to HT1080-LT cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: EZH2 binding was higher at the TERT promoter in HT1080-ST compared to HT1080-LT cells.
source: EZH2 binding was also higher at the TERT promoter in ST compared to HT1080-LT cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: REST and EZH2 occupancy at the TERT promoter was lower in MDA-MB-231-LT compared to MDA-MB-231-ST cells.
source: Similarly, in MDA-MB-231 cells, REST and EZH2 occupancy at the TERT promoter was lower in LT compared to ST cells (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: REST and EZH2 binding at the TERT promoter increased in HCT116-ST relative to HCT116-LT cells.
source: Furthermore, an increase in REST and EZH2 binding at the TERT promoter in ST relative to LT cells was clear in the HCT116-ST/LT cells (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Higher TRF2 binding was observed at the inserted TERT promoter in HEK293T-ST compared to HEK293T-LT cells.
source: Higher TRF2 binding at the inserted TERT promoter in ST compared to the HEK293-LT cells was clear (ChIP-qRT primers specific to the CCR5-TERT insert were used; Figure 4A and C).
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 4C using primers specific to the CCR5 insert.

claim: H3K27me3 deposition was relatively high in HEK293T-ST cells compared to LT cells at the inserted TERT promoter.
source: Consistent with this, H3K27me3 deposition was relatively high in ST cells (Figure 4D), and the TERT promoter-driven Gaussia Luc reporter activity was reduced in the ST relative to the LT cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: TERT promoter-driven Gaussia Luc reporter activity was reduced in HEK293T-ST relative to LT cells.
source: Consistent with this, H3K27me3 deposition was relatively high in ST cells (Figure 4D), and the TERT promoter-driven Gaussia Luc reporter activity was reduced in the ST relative to the LT cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: Demonstrated through luciferase assay shown in Figure 4E.

claim: TL increased to more than fivefold by Day 10 in doxycycline-inducible HT1080 cells.
source: Gradual increase in TL to > fivefold by Day 10 (relative to Day 0) was evident; beyond Day 10, despite dox induction (and relatively high telomerase activity) further TL elongation was not seen (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B; ++/-- denotes presence/absence of dox, respectively).
evidence: Demonstrated through telomere length measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: TL returned to roughly within 1.6-fold of the initial state by Day 24 after withdrawal of doxycycline at Day 10 in HT1080 cells.
source: Following the withdrawal of dox after Day 10, TL returned to roughly within 1.6-fold of the initial (Day 0) state by Day 24 (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated through FACS measurements shown in Figure 5B.

claim: TRF2 binding at the TERT promoter decreased at Day 10 with TL elongation in doxycycline-inducible HT1080 cells.
source: TRF2 binding at the TERT promoter decreased at Day 10 with TL elongation. Conversely, as TL shortened beyond Day 10, TRF2 occupancy on the TERT promoter was regained on Day 24; Figure 5C.
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: TRF2 occupancy on the TERT promoter was regained on Day 24 as TL shortened in doxycycline-inducible HT1080 cells.
source: TRF2 binding at the TERT promoter decreased at Day 10 with TL elongation. Conversely, as TL shortened beyond Day 10, TRF2 occupancy on the TERT promoter was regained on Day 24; Figure 5C.
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: REST and EZH2 occupancy at the TERT promoter decreased on Day 10 relative to Day 0, followed by an increase on Day 24 in doxycycline-inducible HT1080 cells.
source: We then examined the occupancy of REST and EZH2 at the TERT promoter at days 0, 10, and 24: a decrease in occupancy of both REST and EZH2 on Day 10, relative to Day 0, followed by an increase on Day 24 was clear (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: H3K27me3 deposition at the TERT promoter was lower on Day 10 compared to Day 0, followed by an increase on Day 24 in doxycycline-inducible HT1080 cells.
source: Accordingly, H3K27me3 deposition at the TERT promoter was lower on Day 10 compared to Day 0, followed by an increase on Day 24 (Figure 5F).
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Endogenous TERT expression increased by Day 10 from Day 0 levels and was significantly reduced by Day 24 in doxycycline-inducible HT1080 cells.
source: Consistent with this, expression of the endogenous TERT (using 3'UTR specific qRT-PCR primers) increased by Day 10 from Day 0 levels, and was significantly reduced by Day 24 compared to the Day 10 levels, although not reduced to the Day 0 state (Figure 5G), supporting the role of TL elongation in inducing or TL shortening in suppressing TERT.
evidence: Demonstrated through qRT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 5G.

claim: TL elongated to approximately twofold by Day 10 in doxycycline-inducible MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: TL elongated to ~twofold by Day 10; and receded to approximately the initial (Day 0) length by Day 14 after stopping dox at Day 10 (Figure 6B).
evidence: Demonstrated through FACS measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claim: TL receded to approximately the initial length by Day 14 after stopping doxycycline at Day 10 in MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: TL elongated to ~twofold by Day 10; and receded to approximately the initial (Day 0) length by Day 14 after stopping dox at Day 10 (Figure 6B).
evidence: Demonstrated through FACS measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claim: TRF2 binding, REST, EZH2, and H3K27me3 mark at the TERT promoter decreased on Day 10 relative to Day 0 in doxycycline-inducible MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Decrease in TRF2 binding, and corresponding reduced REST, EZH2, and the H3K27me3 mark at the TERT promoter were clear on Day 10 relative to Day 0 (Figure 6C–F).
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 6C-F.

claim: Promoter TRF2, REST, and EZH2 occupancy, including H3K27 trimethylation, was regained at Day 14 relative to Day 10 levels in doxycycline-inducible MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Promoter TRF2, REST, and EZH2 occupancy, including H3K27 trimethylation, was regained in the subsequent time point of Day 14, relative to the Day 10 levels, as expected from TL shortening after Day 10 (Figure 6C–F).
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 6C-F.

claim: Endogenous TERT transcript increased progressively till Day 10 and subsequently reduced gradually at Day 14 in doxycycline-inducible MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Accordingly, we noted endogenous TERT transcript followed TL elongation/shortening: increased progressively till Day 10, and subsequently reduced gradually at Day 14 (Figure 6G).
evidence: Demonstrated through qRT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 6G.

claim: TL was overall higher in all HT1080-LT tumours compared to HT1080-ST tumours in xenograft mice.
source: Following harvesting, tumours were first characterized: TL was overall higher in all LT tumours compared to HT1080-ST tumours; increased TERT and telomerase activity was retained in HT1080-LT tumours relative to ST (Figure 7B and C; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated through qRT-PCR-based telomere length measurements shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Increased TERT and telomerase activity was retained in HT1080-LT tumours relative to ST in xenograft mice.
source: Following harvesting, tumours were first characterized: TL was overall higher in all LT tumours compared to HT1080-ST tumours; increased TERT and telomerase activity was retained in HT1080-LT tumours relative to ST (Figure 7B and C; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated through qRT-PCR and TRAP assay shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: HT1080-ST xenograft tumours had significantly more TRF2 occupancy at the TERT promoter than HT1080-LT tumours.
source: TRF2-ChIP from tumour tissue showed HT1080-ST had significantly more TRF2 occupancy at the TERT promoter than HT1080-LT, consistent with results from cultured cells (Figures 7D and 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR from xenograft tumour tissue shown in Figure 7D.

claim: H3K27me3 mark deposition was reduced in xenograft HT1080-LT tumours compared to HT1080-ST.
source: Correspondingly, H3K27me3 mark deposition was reduced in xenograft HT1080-LT tumours compared to HT1080-ST (Figure 7E), supporting that TL-dependent TERT regulation was retained in cells growing in vivo.
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR from xenograft tumour tissue shown in Figure 7E.

claim: G-quadruplex DNA secondary structures were found in the TERT promoter.
source: G-quadruplex (G4) DNA secondary structures (Bryan and Baumann, 2011), widely reported as gene regulatory motifs (Rawal et al., 2006; Huppert and Balasubramanian, 2007; Verma et al., 2008; Verma et al., 2009), were found in the TERT promoter (Palumbo et al., 2009; Lim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited references.

claim: G>A mutations at –124 or –146 positions from the TSS of the TERT promoter are frequently found to be clinically associated with multiple cancers.
source: G>A mutations at –124 or –146 positions from the TSS of the TERT promoter are frequently found to be clinically associated with multiple cancers and reported to disrupt the G4s (Akincilar et al., 2016b; Huang et al., 2013; Horn et al., 2013; Killela et al., 2013; Kang et al., 2016; Li et al., 2016; Akincilar et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited references.

claim: TRF2 binding at the TERT promoter with G4-disrupting mutations was not regained upon shortening of TL.
source: TRF2 binding at the TERT promoter with G4-disrupting mutations was not regained upon shortening of TL and was consistent in the case of both –124G>A and –146 G>A mutations (Figure 8C, left and right panels).
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The difference in H3K27me3 deposition was insignificant in –124G>A or –146 G>A ST cells compared to the corresponding LT cells.
source: As expected, the difference in H3K27me3 deposition and Gaussia Luc activity was insignificant in –124G>A or –146 G>A ST cells compared to the corresponding LT cells (Figure 8D and E).
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The difference in Gaussia Luc activity was insignificant in –124G>A or –146 G>A ST cells compared to the corresponding LT cells.
source: As expected, the difference in H3K27me3 deposition and Gaussia Luc activity was insignificant in –124G>A or –146 G>A ST cells compared to the corresponding LT cells (Figure 8D and E).
evidence: Demonstrated through luciferase assay shown in Figure 8E.

claim: TRF2 silencing induced TERT expression.
source: As expected, TRF2 silencing induced TERT, and re-expression of TRF2-wild type (WT) repressed TERT.
evidence: Demonstrated through TRF2 knockdown and overexpression experiments.

claim: Re-expression of TRF2-wild type (WT) repressed TERT.
source: As expected, TRF2 silencing induced TERT, and re-expression of TRF2-wild type (WT) repressed TERT.
evidence: Demonstrated through TRF2 overexpression experiments.

claim: TRF2-R17H and K176R increased TERT expression.
source: Interestingly, R17H and K176R increased TERT, whereas T188N and K190R gave relatively moderate change (Figure 9—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated through TRF2 mutant overexpression experiments shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The N-terminal domain of TRF2 (with the R17 residue) was shown to interact with G4 DNA.
source: Noting that the N-terminal domain of TRF2 (with the R17 residue) was shown to interact with G4 DNA (Bryan and Baumann, 2011; Pedroso et al., 2009), and also the core histone H3 (Konishi et al., 2016), we focused on understanding the role of TRF2-R17 at the TERT promoter.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited references.

claim: The N-terminal domain of TRF2 (with the R17 residue) was shown to interact with core histone H3.
source: Noting that the N-terminal domain of TRF2 (with the R17 residue) was shown to interact with G4 DNA (Bryan and Baumann, 2011; Pedroso et al., 2009), and also the core histone H3 (Konishi et al., 2016), we focused on understanding the role of TRF2-R17 at the TERT promoter.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited references.

claim: Induction of TRF2-R17H gave significant upregulation of TERT in HT1080, HCT116, and MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Induction of TRF2-R17H gave significant upregulation of TERT; whereas, as expected, TRF2-WT repressed TERT in all three cell lines (Figure 9A, Figure 9—figure supplement 1C); dox dose-dependent TRF2 induction and resultant TERT levels shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1D.
evidence: Demonstrated through doxycycline-inducible TRF2 mutant expression experiments shown in Figure 9A.

claim: TRF2-WT repressed TERT in HT1080, HCT116, and MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Induction of TRF2-R17H gave significant upregulation of TERT; whereas, as expected, TRF2-WT repressed TERT in all three cell lines (Figure 9A, Figure 9—figure supplement 1C); dox dose-dependent TRF2 induction and resultant TERT levels shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1D.
evidence: Demonstrated through doxycycline-inducible TRF2 expression experiments shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The binding of FLAG-tagged-TRF2-R17H on the TERT promoter was insignificant compared to FLAG tagged-TRF2-WT in HT1080 cells.
source: The binding of FLAG-tagged-TRF2-R17H on the TERT promoter was insignificant compared to the FLAG tagged-TRF2-WT in HT1080 cells (Figure 9C).
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 9C.

claim: REST, EZH2 and H3K27me3 occupancy was significantly low on the TERT promoter for TRF2-R17H compared to TRF2-WT.
source: As expected from the loss of TRF2-R17H binding, REST, EZH2 and H3K27me3 occupancy was significantly low on the TERT promoter for TRF2-R17H compared to TRF2-WT (Figure 9D–F).
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 9D-F.

claim: Treatment with purified TRF2-WT gave further increase in H3K27 trimethylation in vitro.
source: Following this, treatment with purified TRF2-WT gave further increase in H3K27 trimethylation, whereas TRF2-R17H did not lead to any significant increase, relative to respective controls (Figure 9G).
evidence: Demonstrated through in vitro histone methyltransferase assay shown in Figure 9G.

claim: TRF2-R17H did not lead to any significant increase in H3K27 trimethylation in vitro.
source: Following this, treatment with purified TRF2-WT gave further increase in H3K27 trimethylation, whereas TRF2-R17H did not lead to any significant increase, relative to respective controls (Figure 9G).
evidence: Demonstrated through in vitro histone methyltransferase assay shown in Figure 9G.

claim: TERT mRNA expression was higher in iPSCs compared to parent FS fibroblast cells.
source: TERT mRNA expression (Figure 10C), telomerase activity (Figure 10D) and relative telomere length (Figure 10E), were confirmed, and as expected were higher in the iPSCs compared to parent FS fibroblast cells.
evidence: Demonstrated through qRT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 10C.

claim: Telomerase activity was higher in iPSCs compared to parent FS fibroblast cells.
source: TERT mRNA expression (Figure 10C), telomerase activity (Figure 10D) and relative telomere length (Figure 10E), were confirmed, and as expected were higher in the iPSCs compared to parent FS fibroblast cells.
evidence: Demonstrated through TRAP assay shown in Figure 10D.

claim: Relative telomere length was higher in iPSCs compared to parent FS fibroblast cells.
source: TERT mRNA expression (Figure 10C), telomerase activity (Figure 10D) and relative telomere length (Figure 10E), were confirmed, and as expected were higher in the iPSCs compared to parent FS fibroblast cells.
evidence: Demonstrated through qPCR-based telomere length measurement shown in Figure 10E.

claim: TRF2 occupancy in iPSCs with longer telomeres was found to be lower on the TERT promoter in comparison to parent fibroblasts.
source: TRF2 occupancy in the iPSCs with longer telomeres was found to be lower on the TERT promoter in comparison to parent fibroblasts (Figure 10F).
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 10F.

claim: Occupancy of REST was reduced in iPSCs compared to FS Fibroblast cells.
source: Furthermore, occupancy of REST (Figure 10G) and the repressor complex protein, EZH2 (Figure 10H) was reduced in the pluripotent stem cells.
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 10G.

claim: Occupancy of EZH2 was reduced in iPSCs compared to FS Fibroblast cells.
source: Furthermore, occupancy of REST (Figure 10G) and the repressor complex protein, EZH2 (Figure 10H) was reduced in the pluripotent stem cells.
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 10H.

claim: The repressor mark H3K27me3 was significantly lower in iPSCs relative to FS Fibroblast cells.
source: Corresponding to the reduced levels of TRF2 occupancy and resultant lower binding of the REST/PRC2 complex on the TERT promoter in the iPSCs, the repressor mark, H3K27me3 was significantly lower relative to FS Fibroblast cells (Figure 10I).
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 10I.

claim: Telomere-specific sgRNA-guided CRISPR-Cas9 resulted in approximately 50% reduction in TL in iPSCs.
source: We used the telomere-specific sgRNA-guided CRISPR-Cas9 to trim telomeres (as reported earlier) (Chen et al., 2013). This resulted in a population of iPSCs with short telomeres ('iPSC-ST';~50% reduction in TL; see Methods, Figure 11A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated through telomere trimming experiments shown in Figure 11B.

claim: TRF2 binding at the TERT promoter increased approximately threefold in telomere-shortened iPSCs compared to unaltered iPSCs.
source: A comparison of TRF2 occupancy between iPSC-ST cells and unaltered iPSCs revealed a marked increase in TRF2 binding at the TERT promoter (~ threefold) in the telomere-shortened cells (Figure 11C).
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 11C.

claim: H3K27me3 deposition increased 1.5-fold in iPSC-ST cells compared to unaltered iPSCs.
source: As expected from this, based on the above findings, we observed an increase (of 1.5-fold) in the deposition of the repressive histone mark H3K27me3 in iPSC-ST cells compared to unaltered iPSCs (Figure 11D).
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 11D.

claim: TERT was significantly reduced in iPSC-ST cells relative to unaltered iPSCs.
source: Further, consistent with these, TERT was significantly reduced in iPSC-ST cells relative to unaltered iPSCs (Figure 11E).
evidence: Demonstrated through qRT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 11E.

claim: Relatively long telomeres induced permissive chromatin at the TERT promoter.
source: Relatively long telomeres induced permissive chromatin at the TERT promoter. Conversely, shorter telomeres led to closed chromatin at the promoter (Figures 3A–B–5D–E, Figure 6D–E).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental results shown in the cited figures.

claim: Shorter telomeres led to closed chromatin at the TERT promoter.
source: Relatively long telomeres induced permissive chromatin at the TERT promoter. Conversely, shorter telomeres led to closed chromatin at the promoter (Figures 3A–B–5D–E, Figure 6D–E).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental results shown in the cited figures.

claim: TRF2 binding at the TERT promoter is non-telomeric because telomere-associated TRF2 would increase with TL elongation and looping, instead of decreasing as observed.
source: Notably, this showed TRF2 binding at the TERT promoter to be temporally controlled as a function of TL. Second, this further showed that TERT promoter-bound TRF2 was non-telomeric because telomere-associated TRF2 would increase with TL elongation (and looping), instead of decreasing as seen here.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the observation that TRF2 binding decreases when telomeres elongate.

claim: Long telomeres sequester more TRF2 for telomere protection, which reduces TRF2 at the TERT promoter.
source: Long telomeres sequester more TRF2 for telomere protection, which reduces TRF2 at the TERT promoter. Resulting in de-repression of TERT, and increased TERT levels in turn synthesize (Figures 2—4) and help maintain longer telomeres.
evidence: This is a mechanistic summary based on the TSP model and experimental results.

claim: Increased TERT levels synthesize and help maintain longer telomeres.
source: Long telomeres sequester more TRF2 for telomere protection, which reduces TRF2 at the TERT promoter. Resulting in de-repression of TERT, and increased TERT levels in turn synthesize (Figures 2—4) and help maintain longer telomeres.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on the known function of TERT and experimental results.

claim: The findings suggest a feed-forward model mechanistically connecting telomeres to TERT.
source: Taken together, these suggest a feed-forward model mechanistically connecting telomeres to TERT with likely significant implications in better understanding telomere-related physiological events, particularly tumorigenesis, ageing, and de-differentiation (Roake and Artandi, 2020; Vinayagamurthy et al., 2020; Jafri et al., 2016; Wong and Collins, 2003; Muñoz et al., 2006; Rossiello et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: TRF2 has a direct function in histone H3K27 trimethylation in presence of the PRC2 complex.
source: Interestingly, together these support a direct function of TRF2 in histone H3K27 trimethylation in presence of the PRC2 complex, where the R17 residue of TRF2 plays a necessary role.
evidence: Demonstrated through in vitro histone methyltransferase assay showing TRF2-WT enhances H3K27me3 while R17H mutant does not.

claim: The R17 residue of TRF2 plays a necessary role in H3K27 trimethylation.
source: Interestingly, together these support a direct function of TRF2 in histone H3K27 trimethylation in presence of the PRC2 complex, where the R17 residue of TRF2 plays a necessary role.
evidence: Demonstrated through experiments showing TRF2-R17H mutant loses ability to promote H3K27me3.

claim: Telomere length and TERT expression are critical in maintaining pluripotency and the ability of stem cells to differentiate.
source: Telomere length and TERT expression are critical in maintaining pluripotency and the ability of stem cells to differentiate (Flores et al., 2008; Allsopp, 2012; Armstrong et al., 2005; Yang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited references.

claim: The re-occupation of TRF2 at the TERT promoter in telomere-shortened iPSCs demonstrates the applicability of TRF2-dependent TL-sensitive TERT regulation in stem cells.
source: The re-occupation of TRF2 at the TERT promoter in telomere-shortened iPSCs (iPSC-ST) along with suppression of its expression demonstrates the applicability of TRF2-dependent TL-sensitive TERT regulation in stem cells and presents a potentially useful tool to modulate its differentiation capacity and pluripotency with further exploration.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the iPSC experiments and their implications.

claim: TPE-OLD and TSP models are likely context-specific.
source: These support TERT promoter-bound TRF2 as non-telomeric and indicate the two models (TPE-OLD and TSP) are likely context-specific.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the current findings with previously published TPE-OLD mechanism.

claim: Additional experimentation would be required to ascertain the contexts or range of telomere length at which TPE-OLD and TSP mechanisms could operate in isolation or concert.
source: However, additional experimentation would be required to ascertain the contexts or range of telomere length at which the two mechanisms could operate in isolation or concert – providing further insights into their physiological relevance.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: Activation of TERT in many cancers was reported to be frequently due to TERT promoter mutations that overlap with the TERT promoter G4-forming stretch.
source: Interestingly, in many cancers, activation of TERT was reported to be frequently due to TERT promoter mutations; subsequently noted to overlap with the TERT promoter G4-forming stretch (Akincilar et al., 2016b; Sharma and Chowdhury, 2022; Palumbo et al., 2009; Lim et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2013; Horn et al., 2013; Killela et al., 2013; Li et al., 2016; Akincilar et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited references.

claim: The artificially introduced TERT promoter-reporter on G4 disruption lost its dependence on TL.
source: The artificially introduced TERT promoter-reporter on G4 disruption lost its dependence on TL (Figures 4 and 8).
evidence: Demonstrated through experiments with G4-disrupting mutations shown in Figures 4 and 8.

claim: Results from xenograft mice tumours indicated TL-induced TERT activation might be active in vivo.
source: Xenograft mice tumours indicated TL-induced TERT activation might be active in vivo. However, results are primarily from cells engineered for TL elongation/shortening (Figure 7).
evidence: Demonstrated through xenograft experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: It is not clear how the initial TL elongation is triggered during tumorigenic transformation.
source: For example, it is not clear how the initial TL elongation (which results in TERT reactivation) is triggered during tumorigenic transformation.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations and unknowns in the current understanding.

claim: Telomere transfer from antigen-presenting cells results in telomere elongation of specific T cell populations and subsequent telomerase expression induced proliferative expansion during T cell activation.
source: Interestingly, recent work shows telomere transfer from antigen-presenting cells (APCs) results in telomere elongation of specific T cell populations, subsequent telomerase expression induced proliferative expansion during T cell activation (Lanna et al., 2022).
evidence: This refers to recently published work by others.

claim: Telomere transfer between tumour and immune/other cells within the tumour microenvironment might alter TL, contributing to TERT activation.
source: This suggests the possibility of telomere transfer between tumour and immune/other cells within the tumour microenvironment might alter TL, contributing to TERT activation.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the cited work on telomere transfer in T cells.

claim: A similar model of telomere transfer might be functional during reprogramming.
source: A similar model might be functional during reprogramming.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis extending the telomere transfer concept to reprogramming.

claim: It would be of interest to test how TL-dependent TERT regulatory mechanisms affect senescing primary cells and telomerase-negative cancer cells with ALT mechanism.
source: Moreover, it would be of interest to test how TL-dependent TERT regulatory mechanisms affect senescing primary cells and telomerase-negative cancer cells (with ALT mechanism).
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: The remaining shelterin complex components may play crucial roles in telomere length-dependent TERT regulation.
source: The remaining shelterin complex components—POT1, hRap1, TRF1, TIN2, and TPP1—may play crucial roles in this context, as they are integral to telomere maintenance and protection (Stewart et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential roles of other shelterin proteins.

claim: Several DNA damage response proteins could potentially influence TERT regulation in a telomere length-dependent manner.
source: Additionally, several DNA damage response (DDR) proteins, which interact with telomere-binding factors and help preserve telomere integrity, could potentially influence TERT regulation in a telomere length-dependent manner (Longhese, 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential roles of DDR proteins.

claim: Sirtuins directly associate with telomeres and are known to positively regulate telomere length.
source: Another group of proteins with potential relevance in this mechanism are the sirtuins, which directly associate with telomeres and are known to positively regulate telomere length, undergoing repression upon telomere shortening (Amano and Sahin, 2019b; Amano et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited references.

claim: SIRT1 has been reported to interact with telomerase.
source: Notably, SIRT1 has been reported to interact with telomerase (Lee et al., 2024), while SIRT6 has been implicated in TRF2 degradation (Rizzo et al., 2017) and telomerase activation (Chen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited references.

claim: SIRT6 has been implicated in TRF2 degradation.
source: Notably, SIRT1 has been reported to interact with telomerase (Lee et al., 2024), while SIRT6 has been implicated in TRF2 degradation (Rizzo et al., 2017) and telomerase activation (Chen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited references.

claim: SIRT6 has been implicated in telomerase activation.
source: Notably, SIRT1 has been reported to interact with telomerase (Lee et al., 2024), while SIRT6 has been implicated in TRF2 degradation (Rizzo et al., 2017) and telomerase activation (Chen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited references.

claim: Sirtuins may serve as key mediators of telomere length-dependent TERT regulation.
source: Given their roles in telomere homeostasis, sirtuins may serve as key mediators of telomere length-dependent TERT regulation.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on known roles of sirtuins.

claim: The findings suggest a feed-forward model with likely significant implications in better understanding tumorigenesis, ageing, and de-differentiation.
source: Taken together, these suggest a feed-forward model mechanistically connecting telomeres to TERT with likely significant implications in better understanding telomere-related physiological events, particularly tumorigenesis, ageing, and de-differentiation (Roake and Artandi, 2020; Vinayagamurthy et al., 2020; Jafri et al., 2016; Wong and Collins, 2003; Muñoz et al., 2006; Rossiello et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion with speculative implications for future research.
